item.text: {"question_id":"4B.10","answer":"For the 2023 target period, the evidence does not establish that Félix Tshisekedi left political freedom and democratic resilience durably stronger than inherited. There were potentially constructive formal and partial institutional measures: a mixed five-member international expert audit of the voter register, five enacted laws concerning Indigenous Peoples, human-rights defenders, sexual-violence reparations, trafficking, and penitentiary principles, recruitment and training of 2,500 magistrates, expanded justice access, selected mobile-court judgments, and one peaceful October protest that police escorted. These measures show some formal reform, institutional activity, and limited operational space, but they do not demonstrate independent reviewability, nationwide implementation, durable effects, or freedom-enhancing self-binding. The register audit was published by CENI and relied partly on CENI’s internal audit; the justice outputs were materially UNDP-supported and selected; the government’s own submission reported an inquiry whose findings were not yet available; and the protest report does not show consistent protection or policy impact. [BATCH-0023-E015, BATCH-0009-E004, BATCH-0011-E003, BATCH-0022-E014] Judicial reorganization is also ambiguous: presidential ordinances in August 2023 revoked, retired, reassigned, and appointed judges and prosecutors across major courts, while the presidency presented the changes as rule-of-law reform. Without reasons for removals or independent evidence of subsequent judicial independence, these personnel actions complicate rather than establish institutional strengthening. [BATCH-0015-E006, BATCH-0019-E006] The adverse trajectory is stronger on the central resilience mechanisms. The state of siege, enforced and repeatedly extended under Tshisekedi, replaced elected civilian authorities with military and police officials, suspended elected provincial assemblies, authorized military courts to prosecute civilians, and was reported to have restricted rights, harassed or jailed journalists, and detained critics; the authorities also failed to meet an international notification requirement for derogations. [BATCH-0012-R03-E003, BATCH-0012-R03-E004, BATCH-0012-R03-E007] The 2023 election was competitive in form and had some inclusive features, but independent assessments found violence, ruling-coalition administrative-resource abuse, under-registration, incomplete and nontransparent auditing, logistical failures, restricted observation of tabulation, cancelled voting in conflict-affected territories, underrepresentation of women and other groups, and serious credibility defects. Reform recommendations from the prior cycle were reportedly implemented only narrowly, while CENI and the Constitutional Court remained perceived as politicized. [BATCH-0001-E012, BATCH-0001-E014, BATCH-0013-E010, BATCH-0013-E011, BATCH-0028-E014, BATCH-0028-E018] Political information and civic accountability also remained weak: RSF described an insufficiently independent national broadcaster, pressure on journalists, arrests, threats, disappearances, attacks, self-censorship, and impunity; Human Rights Watch reported a broader first-term narrowing of civic space, detention and judicial harassment of critics and journalists, excessive force against demonstrations, and unresolved accountability for security-force abuses. [BATCH-0025-E008, BATCH-0028-E015] Transitional-justice consultations and selected prosecutions did not yield concrete, comprehensive accountability, and the justice system remained dysfunctional because of corruption, political and military interference, and resource shortages. [BATCH-0010-E016, BATCH-0028-E017, BATCH-0028-E018] The reported 12% decline in documented human-rights violations is a qualified favorable indicator, not proof of stronger democratic resilience: it concerns recorded incidents, follows an existing trend, and may reflect conflict and reporting conditions rather than ruler-attributable institutional improvement. [BATCH-0025-E009] Thus, the record supports formal reform and partial capacity alongside substantial erosion or non-remedy of contestability, civic space, independent constraints, and accountability. The March and July 2024 publications are used retrospectively for 2023 outcomes and first-term trajectory; they do not extend the judgment period. Causation remains limited because many abuses involved collective state institutions, security forces, parties, armed groups, or conflict conditions rather than proven personal presidential direction, and external partners materially contributed to some favorable outputs. Durability beyond 2023 is not demonstrated.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0023-E015","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0011-E003","BATCH-0022-E014","BATCH-0015-E006","BATCH-0019-E006","BATCH-0025-E009"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-R03-E003","BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0012-R03-E007","BATCH-0001-E012","BATCH-0001-E014","BATCH-0013-E010","BATCH-0013-E011","BATCH-0028-E014","BATCH-0028-E015","BATCH-0025-E008","BATCH-0010-E016","BATCH-0028-E017","BATCH-0028-E018","BATCH-0026-E012","BATCH-0002-E013"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied record does not establish a counterfactual against inherited conditions or prove durable effects beyond 2023.","Formal laws, staffing, audits, and selected justice outputs do not establish independent reviewability, nationwide implementation, or institutional durability.","Several adverse findings concern government institutions, security forces, political parties, or armed groups collectively and do not prove Tshisekedi personally ordered each act.","The CENI audit and government submission are self-reported or institutionally interested accounts; the audit also relied on CENI internal material.","The 12% decline measures documented violations, not all violations or democratic resilience, and may reflect conflict and reporting conditions.","The March and July 2024 sources assess 2023 retrospectively; they are not contemporaneous evidence and do not expand the target period.","The record is weak on peaceful transfer, correction of abuses, consistent nationwide civic protections, and independently verified long-term institutional outcomes."],"corrections_made":["Reduced the favorable weight assigned to the CENI audit, UNDP-supported justice outputs, and the recorded decline in violations by stating their source, attribution, and durability limitations.","Added the August 2023 presidential judicial appointments, removals, retirements, and reassignments and explained why they complicate claims of independent institutional strengthening.","Added the independent press-freedom evidence and connected it to political information, civic space, and accountability.","Added explicit retrospective-period labeling for the March and July 2024 assessments.","Preserved favorable evidence, contrary evidence, attribution limits, conflict constraints, and the absence of a counterfactual without converting the answer into a score."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["Independent evidence on the reasons for judicial removals and appointments, subsequent judicial decisions, and actual institutional independence could materially change the trajectory assessment.","Evidence after 2023 demonstrating durable correction, accountability, electoral reform implementation, or strengthened independent reviewability would clarify whether the partial reforms persisted.","A fuller comparative baseline for inherited political freedom and the effects of conflict, armed-group control, and external assistance would improve causal attribution."]}
